title: Reconstruct AlexNet
summary: Trace the design choices that made deep convolutional networks practical, then implement convolution and pooling from first principles.

parts.title: Why local receptive fields?
parts.prompt: Why does AlexNet use small learned kernels instead of connecting every image pixel directly to every hidden unit?
parts.answer: Convolution shares one kernel across spatial positions. This preserves locality, reduces parameters dramatically, and lets the same feature detector recognize a pattern wherever it appears.
hints: Compare a dense image layer with a 3x3 kernel.
Which image property is preserved by sliding a kernel?

parts.title: Why ReLU instead of tanh?
parts.prompt: Explain why AlexNet replaced saturating activations with ReLU and how this affected optimization.
parts.answer: ReLU has a constant derivative on positive inputs, so it avoids the strong saturation of tanh and sigmoid. AlexNet therefore trained substantially faster while retaining a simple nonlinear decision boundary.
hints: Inspect derivatives for large positive inputs.
Faster optimization was the central benefit.

parts.title: Why overlap pooling and augmentation?
parts.prompt: How did pooling, crops, flips, and color perturbations work together to improve recognition?
parts.answer: Pooling reduced spatial sensitivity and computation, while augmentation exposed the model to label-preserving image variations. Together they encouraged robust features and reduced overfitting in the large network.
hints: Separate architectural invariance from data diversity.
Which operations change the training set without changing labels?

parts.title: Implement multi-channel convolution
parts.prompt: Implement conv2d_forward(x, w, b, stride) for channel-first tensors without padding.

parts.title: Implement max pooling
parts.prompt: Implement max_pool2d(x, size, stride) over each channel independently.
